title: Ar-Rahim, the Especially Merciful
hookLine: the Especially Merciful, mercy close to each one, shaped like a family
tomorrow: if mercy is that close, who's actually in charge here?

lines: THE NURSE WHO LEARNED YOUR NAME.
cards: A hospital is full of care, and still it's the one nurse who learned your name that you remember. A kindness the size of a crowd is easy to miss. So, yesterday's question: does mercy that big ever find just one person?
Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim. Same root, two names, side by side. The second is Ar-Rahim.

teach.b: Scholars have explained the pair this way: Ar-Rahman is mercy as wide as creation; Ar-Rahim is mercy that keeps arriving, close, to this one.

The Qur'an says in Surah al-Ahzab, in Pickthall's words: He is ever Merciful to the believers. And a sacred hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi brings it all the way home. In paraphrase, Allah says: I am ar-Rahman.

teach.h: THE RAHIM, NAMED FROM HIS NAME.
teach.b: I created the rahim, the womb and the ties of family, and gave it a name from My own name. Whoever keeps those ties, I keep him.
So the closest mercy has the shape of a family: the aunt who calls, the cousin you stopped texting. Now a neighbor who says something close.
In the Torah, when God passes before Moses, the words in the 1917 Jewish translation are: The LORD, the LORD, God, merciful and gracious, long-suffering, and abundant in goodness and truth.
Jewish prayer books set those words in prayers for forgiveness.
What's shared: a God described first by mercy, close enough to meet one person.
An honest difference: Muslims meet that mercy as names of Allah, said at the opening of the surahs; Jews meet it as a scene in the Torah, God's own words to Moses on the mountain.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in this sacred hadith, the word for family ties is named after mercy.

how: Muslims treat keeping family ties (silat al-rahim) as a religious duty: visiting, calling and helping relatives, including ones they've drifted from.

o: a prophet who was known for his gentleness
mercy that keeps arriving, close to each one
mercy given only once, on the Last Day

games.q: wide and close — tap the pairs.

s: in the sacred hadith, the word for family ties is named from Ar-Rahman
I created the rahim and gave it a name from My own name.
Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim mean exactly the same thing
same root, but scholars explain one as mercy wide as creation, the other as mercy that keeps arriving, close.
Islam and Judaism describe mercy in the same way and the same setting
both name God by mercy; Muslims meet it as names of Allah, Jews as a scene in the Torah with Moses.

games.q: your cousin hasn't spoken to your family since a fight over money. your mom says, 'leave it, that's their problem.' what does the sacred hadith on the rahim point toward?
o: keeping the tie is close mercy; one small step toward them counts.
mercy is for strangers; family fights sort themselves out in time.
only reach out once they apologize; that's what fairness needs.
games.why: whoever keeps those ties, I keep him. the closest mercy has the shape of a family, and a small step keeps the tie.

practice: Bring to mind one person in your family, by blood or by choice, where the tie has worn thin. Decide one small mercy for them, a call or a message or a favor, and when it could happen.
For the sit, hold their face in mind and let the plan settle.

wordCard.voice: Ar-Rahim: the Especially Merciful, mercy that keeps arriving, close to each one.

orig.note: Arabic: the Especially Merciful, from the same root as Ar-Rahman, r-h-m.

carryVoice: Something to keep: mercy for me, and the same mercy close to the person next to me. Back tomorrow.

sources.q: He is ever Merciful to the believers

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 1694; Jami' al-Tirmidhi 1907 (sacred hadith: I am ar-Rahman; I created the rahim and derived its name from My name; whoever keeps it, I keep him)
